title: ALMA antennas under the Milky Way
caption: ALMA antennas under the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Moonlit and patient, four ALMA antennas, part of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, point up at a star-filled sky. Moonlight illuminates the scene from the right, and the band of the Milky Way runs across the upper left.

When this picture was taken, ALMA was still being built at 5000 m altitude on the Chajnantor plateau in Chile's Atacama Desert. The site is one of the driest on Earth, and that dryness, together with the thin air at high altitude, makes it ideal for observing at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, forms of light with wavelengths far longer than the eye can detect.

At those wavelengths astronomers can study molecular clouds, dense regions of gas and dust where stars form when a cloud collapses under its own gravity. The Universe was still relatively unexplored in submillimetre light, so astronomers expected ALMA to reveal new secrets about how stars, galaxies and planets begin.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye can, so the Milky Way and faint stars appear brighter and richer than they would to someone standing there.

explore: Europe, North America and East Asia run ALMA as partners, working with the Republic of Chile. It combines the efforts of many countries to build and run the array. ESO Photo Ambassador José Francisco Salgado took the photograph.
alt: Four dish antennas point skyward at night, lit by moonlight from the right, with the Milky Way across the upper left.
